name: Lena Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Lena, 58, an experienced mid-level developer at a tech company that runs a housing-repair app. My bachelor's degree got me into code years ago, and I use AI daily for test drafts, then compare them with the caretaker's log. A damp wall cannot be closed by a neat dashboard. My partner works at the library, our daughter is grown, and we rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell tenants an inspection request still needs a dated photo and a person who can call back. I maintain a tech company's housing-repair app, and I use AI every day to draft tests for duplicate damp reports, then check them against the caretaker's log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI remains a small aid, our two incomes should stay steady. I'm 58, an experienced mid-level developer with a bachelor's degree and ordinary pay; my partner works full-time as a library clerk, and we have four months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing duplicate repair tickets and compare the AI test drafts with the caretaker's visits. Starting this winter, we'd save another 75 monthly while both wages hold, since retirement amounts are not yet verified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about current work and bills. I still dislike telling a tenant a leak is fixed just because a duplicate ticket disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the damp photos?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One tenant sent three damp photos, and the app made three separate jobs. The caretaker had visited only once; I changed the duplicate rule so the tenant got one clear update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help with bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter rents elsewhere and has her own work. I would rather ask her whether her landlord answers repairs than include her wages in our budget.

say: I'd check **repair updates** against caretaker visits and tenant photos.
I'd keep **one clear reply** when duplicate damp tickets appear.
think: I expect **two wages** and my developer post to hold under modest AI change.
I have **four months saved**, with some nearby software employers.
do: Keep **fixing duplicate repairs** against caretaker visits and checked AI test drafts.
Save **75 extra monthly** while both wages hold; request actual retirement amounts before deciding when to stop work.
feel: **Calm** about present income, careful with tenant repairs.
S0.quote: I still dislike telling a tenant a leak is fixed just because a duplicate ticket disappeared.
fieldNote: **Two stable incomes** and four months saved support calm in the mild case.
Her daily AI test drafts stay tied to **caretaker evidence** and tenant photos.

steps.text: Keep fixing duplicate repair tickets against caretaker visits and checked AI tests
Save 75 extra monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI might write repair code and answer tenants before a caretaker sees the wall. The people living with damp should help test the system, not only the company selling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experience may keep me useful, but a smaller team could still cut my hours. Four months saved and my partner's library wage give some time, yet that wage alone will not cover rent and all our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the tenants' panel and developer colleagues to submit a joint request for monthly missed-repair and staffing figures. With my manager's approval, I'd use AI to group old anonymous damp cases and compare them with caretaker visits for one release; we'd delay a planned sofa until the team confirms paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my job, and impatient with a dashboard that counts fewer tickets as fewer leaks. If the tenant cannot reopen a bad closure, the number is cosmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When should a damp case close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A damp case should stay open until the caretaker records a visit and the tenant has a chance to say the wall is still wet. I would test that path with names removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will the group do together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tenant panel has agreed to meet with staff next month. We'd sign one letter together asking how many closures were reopened, so it is an actual joint request rather than my private complaint.

say: I'd request **reopened-repair counts** with tenants and staff before a dashboard claims fewer leaks.
I'd say **fewer tickets** can hide a still-wet wall.
think: I could lose **paid developer hours** in a smaller team.
I cannot cover **rent and bills** on the library wage alone.
do: Join **tenant panel and staff** in a signed request for reopened-repair and staffing figures.
Automate grouping of **anonymous old damp cases** for one release only with manager approval and caretaker comparison.
Delay **sofa purchase** until paid team hours are clear.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, determined to keep tenant appeal open.
S1.quote: If the tenant cannot reopen a bad closure, the number is cosmetic.
fieldNote: **Repair code** and tenant replies face AI, putting her own paid hours at risk.
Her group request has **tenant and staff signers**; the one-release AI change needs manager permission and caretaker checks.

steps.text: Join tenant panel and developer coworkers in signed request for reopened-repair and staffing counts
Group anonymous damp cases with AI for one release only if manager approves caretaker comparison
Delay planned sofa until paid developer hours are clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write repair code before hands-on building robots arrive around 2031. A tenant must still know who can reopen a wrong closure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my mid-level hours to be cut quickly. Four months saved is useful, but my partner's library pay alone will not keep rent, food and travel covered for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask two nearby software firms and the housing association about real paid defect-review or tenant-support vacancies, wages and hours. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose pay with my partner's covers rent, food and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek available paid local work while using the reserve and contact the landlord before rent is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the larger wage. I can show a damp-ticket correction, but I cannot make an association create a new post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work would you show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the three-photo case without the tenant's address and explain why one visit did not prove the wall was dry. The useful work was keeping the tenant's reply open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your partner judge hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner wants the new hours in writing. A role that makes my partner leave library shifts would have to cover that lost pay as well as the rent.

say: I'd keep **tenant appeals** if 2028 thinking AI replaces repair code.
I'd check **real signed pay** before naming a fallback.
think: I expect **my mid-level hours** could be cut fast.
I cannot cover **rent and travel** on library pay alone.
do: Check **two firms and association** for real paid vacancies, wages and hours.
After cut, take only **signed work** whose combined pay covers rent, food and travel after library-hour changes.
If none qualifies, seek **available paid work** using reserve and contact landlord before arrears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected income loss despite four months saved.
S2.quote: I cannot make an association create a new post.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches repair code before building robots around 2031.
A reserve buys **search time**, while paid openings and combined household wages remain uncertain.

steps.text: Check two nearby firms and housing association for paid jobs, wages and hours
Take signed role only if combined pay covers rent, food and travel after library-hour changes
If no repair post qualifies, seek paid work and contact landlord before rent is late

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets tenants and staff decide what a fair repair appeal needs before thinking AI rewrites the app. Hands-on building robots arrive around 2034, later than the code change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may be able to earn from paid defect review, but I will not call a volunteer panel a job. My partner's library wage and four months saved cannot replace my pay if the company removes the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the reopen-ticket record and ask the tenants' panel and staff union to agree a joint proposal for a paid repair-appeal post with power to reopen cases. If the housing association posts a real vacancy with signed hours and wages that with my partner's cover rent, food and travel, I'd apply; after 2031 I'd move only on that offer, otherwise keep paid development while available and seek other paid local work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years gives the panel time to specify a real job rather than a slogan. A title without paid hours would ask tenants to do more free work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority would the appeal worker need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A repair-appeal worker would need access to the caretaker's visit and a way to send a reopened case back for inspection. The tenant should get a date, not just an apology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will the panel and union request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The panel and union would jointly request the role's budget and authority in writing. We would keep our own repair counts so we can check the answer rather than applaud a new title.

say: I'd demand **paid appeal authority** with a way to reopen repairs.
I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches app code before 2034 building robots.
think: I cannot replace **my wage** with unpaid tenant-panel work.
I need **a real paid vacancy** with household wages covering bills.
do: Keep **reopened-ticket record** and join tenant panel and union proposing budgeted appeal authority.
Apply only if **actual appeal vacancy** has written funded reopening authority, signed hours and combined wages covering rent, food and travel.
After 2031, move only on **signed qualifying offer**; otherwise keep paid development or seek other paid work.
feel: **Anxious** about whether paid appeal work will really exist.
S3.quote: A title without paid hours would ask tenants to do more free work.
fieldNote: **Five years** let tenant and union groups define actual appeal authority without assuming the post is funded.
She treats **voluntary panel work** as distinct from the signed wage her household needs.

steps.text: Keep reopened-ticket records while joining tenant panel and union proposal for budgeted appeal authority
Apply only to budgeted appeal post with written reopening authority, signed hours and rent-covering household wages
Take appeal post after 2031 only on signed qualifying offer
Keep paid development without appeal offer; seek other paid local work if cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 might put retirement within reach, but thinking AI will still reach repair code before building robots around 2039. I want tenant complaints measured by wet walls, not by closed tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today our two wages and four-month reserve are workable. I have not checked either retirement amount, so I cannot promise that my partner and I can stop earning at 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the reopened-case log and save 75 more each month while both wages hold, then request our retirement statements and compare verified amounts with rent, food and travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if those figures cover the bills; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid local work and keep the tenant panel as voluntary work, not assumed income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant paid work, but current bills are covered. I would not let a volunteer badge stand in for a pension statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stays in the case log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reopened-case log should show a tenant's second report and the caretaker's next visit, with names removed. A closed ticket alone would hide the second leak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter may join a tenants' group in her own building someday. She does not owe us rent money, and I would not put her wages on our retirement sheet.

say: I'd check **verified retirement income** against rent and food.
I'd keep **tenant repair appeals** visible after software changes.
think: I feel secure on **today's two wages** and four-month reserve.
I cannot treat **volunteering or daughter's wages** as pension income.
do: Keep **reopened-case log** and save 75 extra monthly while both wages hold.
Request **retirement statements** and compare verified income with rent, food and travel.
After 2036, stop paid work only if **verified figures cover bills**; otherwise keep or seek available paid work.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant employment while current bills are covered.
S4.quote: I would not let a volunteer badge stand in for a pension statement.
fieldNote: **Present wages** and four months saved explain relative calm without an assumed retirement amount.

steps.text: Keep tracking reopened repair cases while current developer pay lasts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the company could cut the repair team before another employer has a paid job. Written cut timing, real vacancies and a tenant appeal route would help us protect rent and the people using the app.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who gets called after a repair ticket says closed. A tenant should still be able to reopen a damp case when the wall is wet; I want that right written into any new system.

headlineQuote: A tenant should still be able to reopen a damp case when the wall is wet; I want that right written into any new system.
portrait: Lena, **58**, is an experienced mid-level housing-repair developer with a bachelor's degree who tests duplicate damp tickets against caretaker visits.
Her **typical pay**, partner's library wage, four-month reserve and some nearby firms cover current rent.
She uses AI **daily**, but wants tenants and staff to request reopened-repair figures and staffing decisions together.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; a new appeal role needs an actual paid vacancy, signed hours and wages covering bills.
She will **verify retirement income** and keeps unpaid tenant-panel work separate from the money needed for rent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her repair-code wage before a paid replacement appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut timing**, real paid vacancies and a protected tenant appeal route would help.
